q1: SELECT beer.name, min_price, bar FROM beer LEFT OUTER JOIN (SELECT beer, MIN(price) AS min_price FROM serves GROUP BY beer) AS t ON beer.name = t.beer LEFT OUTER JOIN serves ON beer.name = serves.beer AND min_price = serves.price
q2: WITH MinPriceBeer AS (SELECT beer, MIN(price) AS minPrice FROM Serves GROUP BY beer), BarServedMinPrice AS (SELECT s.beer, s.bar, s.price FROM Serves AS s JOIN MinPriceBeer AS mpb ON s.beer = mpb.beer AND s.price = mpb.minPrice) SELECT b.name, bsmp.price, bsmp.bar FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN BarServedMinPrice AS bsmp ON b.name = bsmp.bar

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 uses a subquery in the FROM clause, which can lead to unexpected results if the subquery returns more than one row for a given beer. Q2, on the other hand, uses a common table expression (CTE) to first find the minimum price for each beer and then join this information with the Serves table. This approach avoids the issue of the subquery returning multiple rows and ensures that the join is performed correctly.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should include a beer that is served by multiple bars at different prices. The difference in results will be due to how Q1 handles the subquery when it returns multiple rows for the same beer, while Q2 correctly identifies the minimum price for each beer and joins it with the Serves table.
